questiontext.text: In the Login Flow machine, which state is marked as the initial state?

Authenticating is reached from AwaitingCreds via submit, not directly from Start.
LoggedIn is reached from Authenticating via valid.

questiontext.text: How many model-coverage criteria does the Explorer let you compare in step 2?

feedback.text: Correct — the Explorer compares four criteria.

questiontext.text: For the selected criterion, which three numbers does the Explorer report?

questiontext.text: What does state coverage require, per the Explorer?

answer.text: Every state is visited at least once

feedback.text: Correct — that is the state-coverage obligation.

answer.text: Every transition is fired at least once

feedback.text: That is transition coverage, a stronger criterion.

answer.text: Every pair of adjacent transitions is exercised

feedback.text: That is transition-pair (switch) coverage.

answer.text: Every simple cycle is traversed once

feedback.text: That is all round-trip paths.

generalfeedback.text: The Explorer calls state coverage the weakest criterion: every state is visited at least once, needing only a few short sequences from the initial state.

questiontext.text: What does transition coverage require, per the Explorer?

answer.text: Every transition is fired at least once

feedback.text: Correct — the usual baseline for FSM testing.

answer.text: Every state is visited at least once

feedback.text: That is only state coverage, which transition coverage subsumes.

answer.text: Every incoming/outgoing transition pair is exercised

feedback.text: That is transition-pair (switch) coverage.

answer.text: The shortest closed tour is walked

feedback.text: That is the Chinese-Postman tour, shown separately.

generalfeedback.text: Transition coverage fires every transition at least once; the Explorer notes it subsumes state coverage and is the usual baseline.

questiontext.text: Which criterion does the Explorer describe as the weakest?

feedback.text: Correct — the Explorer calls state coverage the weakest model criterion.
Transition coverage is stronger; it subsumes state coverage.
Switch coverage is stronger still.
Round-trip coverage targets cycles and is not the weakest.

generalfeedback.text: State coverage — "the weakest model criterion" — is met by a few short sequences from the initial state.

questiontext.text: In the Vending Machine model, which transition is a self-loop (source and target the same state)?

questiontext.text: In the ATM Session machine (initial state Idle), which event leaves Idle, and to which state?

feedback.text: Correct — Idle --insertCard--> CardInserted.
enterPIN leaves CardInserted, not Idle.
withdraw leaves MenuShown, not Idle.

questiontext.text: What is the Chinese-Postman transition tour the Explorer shows?

answer.text: The shortest closed walk from the initial state that fires every transition at least once

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly its definition in the Explorer.

answer.text: The shortest path that visits every state once

feedback.text: That would be about states; the tour is about firing every transition.

answer.text: The longest sequence the machine can produce

feedback.text: The tour is the shortest closed walk, not the longest sequence.

answer.text: Any test case generated by transition coverage

feedback.text: The tour is a single shortest closed walk, computed separately from the criteria.

generalfeedback.text: The tour is the shortest closed walk from the initial state firing every transition at least once (a directed Chinese-Postman route).

questiontext.text: The bridge notes that the State Transition Explorer only counts coverage of the same FSM model, while this Explorer actually generates the test sequences.

feedback.text: Correct — same model; one counts coverage, the other generates sequences.

questiontext.text: Under state coverage, the Login suite is: open; open · submit; open · submit · valid; open · submit · tooManyTries. What is the total steps metric?

feedback.text: Correct — 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9 event steps.

11 is the round-trip total steps for Login, not state coverage.

questiontext.text: For the Login machine under transition coverage, how many test cases does the Explorer generate?

answer.text: 1 — a single 10-step walk fires all 7 transitions

feedback.text: Correct — transition coverage weaves all transitions into one sequence.
The generator chains transitions into a single walk, not one test each.

9 is the switch-coverage test count.

questiontext.text: For the Login machine under transition-pair (switch) coverage, how many obligations does the Explorer report?

feedback.text: Correct — summing (incoming × outgoing) over the five states gives 9.
7 is the transition count (transition-coverage obligations), not the pair count.
5 is the state count; switch obligations sum in×out per state.
14 is the Vending machine's switch obligations, not Login's.

name.text: Which criterion gives one Login test

questiontext.text: For the Login machine, which criterion produces exactly one test case?

feedback.text: Correct — it chains all 7 transitions into a single walk (1 test).
State coverage yields 4 test cases for Login.
Switch coverage yields 9 test cases for Login.
Round-trip yields 3 test cases for Login.

generalfeedback.text: Only transition coverage collapses to a single Login test (1 walk / 10 steps); state=4, switch=9, round-trip=3.

questiontext.text: Under all round-trip paths, how many test cases (one per simple cycle) does the Login machine yield?

feedback.text: Correct — the Login model has three simple cycles.
There are three simple cycles, so three round-trip tests.
5 is the state count, not the number of cycles.
7 is the transition count, not the number of cycles.

generalfeedback.text: Round-trip coverage traverses each simple cycle once. Login has three: Start→AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→LoggedIn→Start, Start→AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→Locked→Start, and AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→AwaitingCreds.

questiontext.text: Which criterion is described as catching faults where a transition lands in the wrong state, so the next transition behaves unexpectedly?

feedback.text: Correct — switch coverage pairs an incoming edge with each outgoing edge to expose wrong landings.
State coverage only visits states; it misses broken transitions entirely.
Transition coverage fires each edge alone and can miss the interaction fault.
Round-trip targets loop faults (stale state), not wrong-landing pairs.

generalfeedback.text: The Explorer says switch coverage "catches faults where a transition lands in the wrong state: the next transition then behaves unexpectedly."

questiontext.text: According to the Explorer, achieving transition coverage automatically achieves state coverage, because firing every transition necessarily visits every reachable state.

feedback.text: Correct — transition coverage subsumes state coverage.
The Explorer states transition coverage subsumes state coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Every transition has a source and target state, so exercising all transitions visits all reachable states — transition coverage subsumes state coverage.

questiontext.text: Which criterion is described as catching faults that only surface after a loop — stale state left behind by a previous pass?

feedback.text: Correct — traversing each simple cycle exercises loop and re-entry behavior.
State coverage never forces a loop to repeat.
Transition coverage fires each edge once but need not repeat a cycle.
Switch targets adjacent-pair faults, not stale state after a loop.

generalfeedback.text: Round-trip coverage traverses every simple cycle, so it "catches faults that only surface after a loop: stale state left behind by a previous pass."

questiontext.text: In the ATM machine, which event sequence from Idle reaches the Dispensing state?

feedback.text: Correct — Idle→CardInserted→PINEntered→MenuShown→Dispensing.
That reaches MenuShown; withdraw is still needed to reach Dispensing.
cancel returns to Idle, where withdraw is undefined.
pinWrong returns to CardInserted, where withdraw is undefined.

generalfeedback.text: Dispensing is reached only via MenuShown --withdraw-->, and MenuShown needs pinCorrect after enterPIN: insertCard · enterPIN · pinCorrect · withdraw.

questiontext.text: In the Login machine, after the sequence open · submit · valid from Start, which state is active?

feedback.text: Correct — Start→AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→LoggedIn.
submit reaches Authenticating, but valid then advances to LoggedIn.
Locked is reached via tooManyTries, not valid.
invalid returns to AwaitingCreds; valid does not.

generalfeedback.text: open (Start→AwaitingCreds), submit (→Authenticating), valid (→LoggedIn): the active state is LoggedIn.

name.text: Why open alone misses state coverage

questiontext.text: Why does the single sequence open fail to achieve state coverage of the Login machine?

answer.text: It visits only Start and AwaitingCreds, leaving Authenticating, LoggedIn, and Locked unvisited

feedback.text: Correct — three of the five states are never entered.

answer.text: It fires no transition at all

feedback.text: It fires open; the problem is that most states remain unvisited.

answer.text: It repeats a transition, which is disallowed

feedback.text: Repetition is allowed; the issue is unvisited states.

answer.text: open is an undefined event in Start

feedback.text: open is Start's defined transition; state coverage still fails because most states are unreached.

generalfeedback.text: State coverage requires visiting all five states. open reaches only AwaitingCreds (plus Start), so Authenticating, LoggedIn, and Locked stay unvisited.

name.text: ATM: more tests, transition or switch

questiontext.text: For the ATM machine, which criterion generates more test cases, transition coverage or transition-pair (switch) coverage?

answer.text: Switch coverage — 12 test cases versus transition coverage's 1

feedback.text: Correct — switch coverage's per-state pairing yields far more tests.

answer.text: Transition coverage — it has one test per transition

feedback.text: Transition coverage collapses to a single ATM walk, not one per transition.
Switch yields 12; transition yields 1 — very different.

answer.text: Neither generates any test for ATM

feedback.text: Both do: transition = 1 test, switch = 12 tests.

generalfeedback.text: Stronger criteria cost more: ATM transition coverage is 1 test (13 steps), switch coverage is 12 tests (45 steps).

questiontext.text: In the comparison chart, the Login switch-coverage row shows the label 9 / 33. What do these two numbers mean?

answer.text: 9 test cases and 33 total event steps

feedback.text: Correct — the label is test cases / total steps.
The label is test cases / total steps, not obligations / tests.
Those describe the model, not the suite label.
The label reads test cases (9) then total steps (33).

generalfeedback.text: The compare note says the bar shows total event steps and the label shows test cases / steps — so 9 / 33 is 9 tests and 33 steps.

questiontext.text: For the Login machine, the Chinese-Postman tour has lower bound 7 (transitions) and tour length 10. What is the repeated steps (overhead) value?

feedback.text: Correct — 10 − 7 = 3 repeated steps.
+0 would mean an Eulerian tour; Login's tour is longer than the lower bound.
7 is the lower bound itself, not the overhead.
10 is the tour length; overhead is length minus lower bound.

generalfeedback.text: Overhead = tour length − transitions = 10 − 7 = 3, so the Login tour repeats 3 steps and is not Eulerian.

questiontext.text: Across the four criteria for the Login machine — state (4 tests), transition (1), switch (9), round-trip (3) — which criterion produces the largest suite by test-case count?

feedback.text: Correct — switch coverage's per-state pairing yields the most tests.
4 is fewer than switch coverage's 9.

answer.text: All round-trip paths, with 3 test cases

feedback.text: 3 is fewer than switch coverage's 9.
Transition coverage yields the fewest tests here, not the most.

generalfeedback.text: Switch coverage (9) beats state (4), round-trip (3), and transition (1): pairing every incoming with every outgoing edge multiplies obligations and tests.

questiontext.text: For the Login machine, which criterion produces the fewest test cases, and why?

answer.text: Transition coverage — the generator chains all transitions into a single walk

feedback.text: Correct — 7 transitions become one 10-step test.

answer.text: State coverage — one test suffices for all states

feedback.text: State coverage needs 4 tests here because states lie on divergent branches.

answer.text: Switch coverage — pairs collapse into one test

feedback.text: Switch coverage yields the most tests (9), not the fewest.

answer.text: Round-trip — cycles merge into one test

feedback.text: Round-trip yields one test per cycle (3), not the fewest.

generalfeedback.text: Transition coverage weaves every transition into one connected walk, so Login needs just 1 test (10 steps) — fewer than state (4), round-trip (3), or switch (9).

questiontext.text: The ATM machine has 12 switch obligations. Using (incoming × outgoing) per state, which state contributes the most transition-pair obligations?

feedback.text: Correct — CardInserted has 2 in (insertCard, pinWrong) and 2 out (enterPIN, cancel).
Idle contributes 3, one fewer than CardInserted's 4.
PINEntered contributes only 2.
Dispensing contributes just 1.

generalfeedback.text: Per state: Idle 3×1=3, CardInserted 2×2=4, PINEntered 1×2=2, MenuShown 1×2=2, Dispensing 1×1=1 → total 12; CardInserted (4) is the largest.

questiontext.text: The Vending machine has 14 switch obligations, of which HasCoins alone contributes 3 × 3 = 9. Why is HasCoins's in- and out-degree so high?

answer.text: Its insertMore self-loop counts once as an incoming edge and once as an outgoing edge of HasCoins

feedback.text: Correct — the self-loop inflates both degrees, so in×out grows.

answer.text: HasCoins is the initial state, so every path starts there

feedback.text: Idle is the initial state; degree, not initiality, drives the pair count.

answer.text: HasCoins has a guard that doubles its transitions

feedback.text: This model has no guards; the self-loop is what raises the degree.

answer.text: Switch coverage counts states twice when they repeat

feedback.text: Switch obligations are in×out per state; the self-loop is the reason HasCoins is high.

generalfeedback.text: HasCoins has incoming {insertCoin, insertMore, clearSelection}=3 and outgoing {insertMore, selectItem, cancel}=3. The insertMore self-loop appears in both sets, giving 3×3=9 of the 14 obligations.

name.text: Why Login tour is not Eulerian

questiontext.text: The Login tour reports length 10 against a lower bound of 7 (not Eulerian). What does that gap indicate about the model?

answer.text: Some states have unequal in- and out-degree, so certain transitions must be repeated to close the walk

feedback.text: Correct — degree imbalance forces the +3 repeated steps.

answer.text: The machine has an unreachable transition

feedback.text: All transitions are reachable; the gap is from degree imbalance, not unreachability.

answer.text: There are 3 states that were never visited

feedback.text: The tour fires every transition and visits every state; the +3 is repeated steps.

answer.text: Transition coverage failed to generate a suite

feedback.text: It generated a 10-step walk; the point is the tour exceeds the lower bound by 3.

generalfeedback.text: A directed tour equals the transition count only when every vertex is balanced (in-degree = out-degree). Login is unbalanced, so 3 transitions must repeat: length 10 = 7 + 3.

questiontext.text: Login's transition-coverage suite is a single walk of 10 steps, yet the machine has only 7 transitions. Why are there 10 steps, not 7?

answer.text: The walk cannot chain all 7 transitions without revisiting already-covered edges to reach the remaining uncovered ones

feedback.text: Correct — reconnecting to uncovered transitions costs extra, already-fired steps.

answer.text: Each transition is deliberately fired twice for reliability

feedback.text: The generator fires each transition at least once, not twice by design.

answer.text: Three transitions are self-loops that count double

feedback.text: Login has no self-loops; the extra steps come from reconnecting walks.

answer.text: The suite includes 3 extra tests of one step each

feedback.text: It is a single test of 10 steps, not multiple tests.

generalfeedback.text: After firing a branch (e.g. reaching LoggedIn then logout), the walk must return through covered transitions to reach still-uncovered ones (invalid, tooManyTries, resetByAdmin), adding 3 repeated steps for a 10-step total.

questiontext.text: For ATM, transition coverage is 8 obligations / 1 test / 13 steps while switch coverage is 12 obligations / 12 tests / 45 steps. Which reading of this trade-off matches the Explorer's note?

answer.text: Switch coverage targets more (interaction) fault types but costs much more to run

feedback.text: Correct — stronger criteria find more faults at higher suite cost.

answer.text: Transition coverage is strictly better because it is cheaper

feedback.text: Cheaper, but it misses the interaction faults switch coverage targets.

answer.text: Switch coverage is cheaper because it has fewer steps

feedback.text: Switch has more steps (45 vs 13), not fewer.

answer.text: The two suites detect exactly the same faults

feedback.text: Switch adds adjacent-pair (wrong-landing) faults that transition coverage can miss.

generalfeedback.text: The compare note: stronger criteria find more faults but cost more to run. Switch's 12 tests / 45 steps buy adjacent-pair fault detection over transition coverage's cheaper 1 test / 13 steps.

questiontext.text: In the Login comparison chart, switch coverage totals 33 steps and round-trip totals 11 steps. Since the bar encodes total steps, which row has the longer bar?

feedback.text: Correct — the bar length is proportional to total steps.
Round-trip totals 11 steps here, shorter than switch's 33.
33 and 11 differ, so the bars differ.

answer.text: Neither has a bar; only the label is shown

feedback.text: Each row draws a bar whose width is total steps relative to the max.

generalfeedback.text: The bar width is (row total steps / max total steps). Switch (33) draws a longer bar than round-trip (11).

questiontext.text: Login's state-coverage suite is open; open · submit; open · submit · valid; open · submit · tooManyTries. Which transition does this suite never fire?

feedback.text: Correct — the suite reaches LoggedIn but never fires logout.
valid is fired by the third test.
submit is fired by three of the tests.
tooManyTries is fired by the fourth test.

generalfeedback.text: The suite fires open, submit, valid, and tooManyTries. It never fires invalid, logout, or resetByAdmin — so logout is one it misses, illustrating that state coverage does not imply transition coverage.

name.text: Why Login state coverage needs 4 tests

questiontext.text: State coverage of Login yields 4 test cases, not 1. What best explains needing more than one sequence?

answer.text: The model branches — LoggedIn and Locked lie on divergent paths, so one non-repeating walk cannot enter both

feedback.text: Correct — separate short sequences are needed to reach states on different branches.

answer.text: Each state must be visited by its own dedicated test

feedback.text: One walk can cover several states; the split comes from branching, not a one-test-per-state rule.

answer.text: State coverage forbids sequences longer than one event

feedback.text: Sequences can be several events long (e.g. open · submit · valid).

answer.text: The initial state must be re-entered between tests

feedback.text: The reason is divergent branches, not a re-entry rule.

generalfeedback.text: From Start the generator extends toward the nearest unvisited state each round; because LoggedIn (via valid) and Locked (via tooManyTries) are on different branches out of Authenticating, distinct short sequences are needed — 4 tests, 9 steps.

questiontext.text: Round-trip coverage traverses each simple cycle. Which of the following is a simple cycle in the Login machine?

feedback.text: Correct — submit then invalid returns to AwaitingCreds.
There is no transition from AwaitingCreds back to Start, so this is not a cycle.
There is no LoggedIn → Locked transition, and it does not return to its start.
There is no transition between Locked and LoggedIn.

generalfeedback.text: Login's simple cycles are Start→AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→LoggedIn→Start, Start→AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→Locked→Start, and AwaitingCreds→Authenticating→AwaitingCreds (submit, invalid).

questiontext.text: The Chinese-Postman tour overheads are: Login +3 (7→10), ATM +5 (8→13), Vending +2 (7→9). Which machine has the largest repeated-steps overhead?

feedback.text: Correct — ATM's degree imbalance forces the most repeats.
+3 is less than ATM's +5.
+2 is the smallest overhead, not the largest.
They differ: +3, +5, +2.

generalfeedback.text: Overhead = tour length − transitions: Login 10−7=3, ATM 13−8=5, Vending 9−7=2. ATM's +5 is largest, and none of the three tours is Eulerian.

questiontext.text: The Explorer flags a transition tour as Eulerian only when the overhead is +0 — the tour length equals the transition-count lower bound, so every transition is fired exactly once.

feedback.text: Correct — Eulerian requires zero repeated steps (tour length = lower bound).
The Explorer labels a tour Eulerian exactly when overhead is +0 and the walk closes.

generalfeedback.text: A tour is Eulerian when extra = 0 and the walk closes — the tour equals the lower bound and each transition fires once. None of the three sample FSMs is Eulerian.

questiontext.text: Suppose ATM's pinCorrect should reach MenuShown but a bug lands it in CardInserted. Which criterion is designed to expose this, and why does plain transition coverage risk missing it?

answer.text: Switch coverage — it pairs the incoming pinCorrect with each edge leaving MenuShown, so the wrong landing derails the next transition; transition coverage fires pinCorrect once in isolation and may not check what follows

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly the adjacent-pair fault switch coverage targets.

answer.text: State coverage — visiting MenuShown reveals the bug

feedback.text: If pinCorrect lands elsewhere, MenuShown may still be visited another way; visiting a state does not check the landing edge.

answer.text: Round-trip coverage — only loops expose it

feedback.text: The fault is an adjacent-pair (wrong-landing) fault, which switch coverage targets, not specifically a loop fault.

answer.text: No criterion here can catch it

feedback.text: Switch coverage is specifically designed for wrong-landing faults.

generalfeedback.text: Transition coverage fires pinCorrect alone and may not exercise what should follow in MenuShown. Switch coverage pairs pinCorrect with each MenuShown outgoing edge (withdraw, cancelAtMenu), so a wrong landing makes the next transition behave unexpectedly — the fault class the Explorer attributes to switch coverage.

questiontext.text: Why does transition-pair (switch) coverage generally require more test cases than plain transition coverage?

answer.text: It must exercise every pair of adjacent transitions, so a state with i incoming and o outgoing transitions contributes i×o obligations

feedback.text: Correct — pairing incoming with outgoing edges multiplies obligations per state.

answer.text: It must visit every state at least once, which transition coverage skips

feedback.text: Transition coverage already visits every reachable state; that is not the reason.

answer.text: It needs a Chinese-Postman tour, which transition coverage does not

feedback.text: The tour is separate from switch coverage; the driver is the i×o pairing.

answer.text: It generates one test per transition, but makes each test twice as long

feedback.text: The growth is in obligation count (i×o per state), not test length.

generalfeedback.text: Switch coverage multiplies in-degree by out-degree at every state, so obligations — and the suite — grow far faster than one-per-transition. For Login this is 9 obligations / 9 tests versus transition coverage's 7 obligations / 1 test.
